items.title: Earl May interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 11, 2001
items.q: I was playing with Billy Taylor’s trio at the time... Billy asked me to open Birdland with him and make all these gigs, and be a steady member of his trio

ctx.x: It makes for a good story. You were absorbing it. But you found the bass eventually.

Yeah that was by accident also. Because I always felt that I could see myself up there like a Buddy Rich or a Gene Krupa or some great drummer, with the spotlight on him you know, and all the girls looking at you you know, and that’d be great. So I would take my little allowance you know and go down on 42nd Street, and a Wurlitzer, and take drum lessons on Saturday. And when I got to high school I was going to study the drums. But when I got there — oh Sonny Payne was in that school at that time, and he was like…

had no idea that I would have any kind of career like I’ve had you know. I played with Charlie Parker and Billy Taylor and Miles Davis’ band and I’ve had all kinds of great, wonderful experiences you know, Dizzy Gillespie and all that stuff. So had I thought I probably would have —

items.title: Billy Taylor — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: My first, really when I began to support a trio and began to get out there with a trio, the trio was Earl May and Charlie Smith. And we worked together for a long time.

ctx.x: Yeah give me the current… because we left it…

My first, really when I began to support a trio and began to get out there with a trio, the trio was Earl May and Charlie Smith. And we worked together for a long time. But Charlie Smith unfortunately had a drinking habit and so he had the dubious distinction of having been hired and fired by every major pianist in jazz, literally. I mean there was hardly a pianist that you couldn’t mention, Earl Garner, Oscar Peterson, Art Tatum, Duke Ellington I mean there was no one you could mention that he hadn’t played with…

and I don’t… it doesn’t sound right with me.” He said, “I can do that.” I said, “Well you don’t have a Congo drum.” He said, “Yeah but I can do that.” So he took the mallet and began [music sounds] and he invented that in that context. Nobody had done that before Charlie Smith. And the reason he did it because he wanted me to play this tune. And ultimately he got a Congo drum and put that in between… he would move his snare over and play the Congo and work both feet and use his hands on the Congo and do like…
